1E (Groups, Rings and Modules)

Words: 162 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 162
1E OurBigBook.com
A permutation representation is a group homomorphism ρ:G→Sym(Ω), equivalently a group action on a set Ω. The left regular action takes Ω=G and ρ(g)(h)=gh. Each such map is a bijection, and ρ(g1​g2​)=ρ(g1​)ρ(g2​). If ρ(g) is the identity, evaluating at the identity element gives g=1. Thus the representation is faithful. Numbering the elements of G identifies Sym(G) with the symmetric group Sn​, proving Cayley theorem:
G≅ρ(G)≤Sn​.​
(1)
For a nonabelian simple group, compose this faithful representation with the sign of a permutation homomorphism Sn​→{1,−1}. Its kernel is a normal subgroup of G, hence either trivial or all of G. A trivial kernel would embed G in a group of order two, contradicting noncommutativity. Therefore every represented element is even, and the same representation embeds G in the alternating group An​.
Finally let S3​ act on the two cosets of its normal subgroup A3​. An even permutation fixes both cosets, whereas an odd permutation exchanges them. This gives S3​→S2​ with kernel A3​; explicitly, send even permutations to the identity and odd permutations to (12).

3E (Metric and Topological Spaces)

Words: 231 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 231
3E OurBigBook.com
The convention in this question counts a point whenever every open neighbourhood meets A, without excluding the point itself. These are adherent points, whose set is the closure A; they differ from limit points under the convention that requires a different point of A in each neighbourhood.
If A is a closed set and x∈/A, the open set X∖A is a neighbourhood of x disjoint from A. Thus every adherent point lies in A. Conversely, if every adherent point lies in A, each x∈/A has an open neighbourhood disjoint from A. Their union is X∖A, which is open. Hence A is closed exactly when it contains all the points specified in the question.
The interior of a set and closure are
Int(A)=⋃{U:U open, U⊆A},A=⋂{F:F closed, A⊆F}.​
(7)
The neighbourhood description of the closure follows because failure to be adherent is equivalent to lying in an open set disjoint from A.
For closure of a connected set, suppose A=U⊔V were a separation into two nonempty relatively open sets. Their intersections with the connected subset A would separate A unless one intersection were empty. Say A⊆U. Choose v∈V and an open set O⊆X with v∈O and O∩A⊆V. Since v∈A, the set O meets A, contradicting A⊆U. Thus the closure of a connected set is connected. The empty-set case holds directly.

V−E+F=2,​

Let p and h count the pentagonal and hexagonal faces. Counting incidences of edges with vertices and faces gives
3V=2E,5p+6h=2E,F=p+h.
(12)
The Euler formula for a sphere also applies to this polygonal decomposition: triangulating a polygon by adding one diagonal increases both E and F by one, preserving V−E+F. Substitution gives
2=32E​−E+p+h=p+h−65p+6h​=6p​.
(13)
Thus there are exactly 12 pentagons, independently of the number of hexagons.

Lift the angular coordinate continuously to a real coordinate and write Δz=zB​−zA​ and Δϕm​=ϕB​−ϕA​+2πm for a prescribed winding number m∈Z. Assume zA​<zB​ for the calculation; reversing the endpoints changes no length. The arc length functional on the circular cylinder is
L[ϕ]=∫zA​zB​​1+R2ϕ′(z)2​dz.
(14)
The Euler-Lagrange equation says R2ϕ′/1+R2ϕ′2​ is constant. This expression is strictly increasing in ϕ′, so ϕ′ is constant. The candidate is the helix
ϕ(z)=ϕA​+ΔzΔϕm​​(z−zA​),Lm​=Δz2+R2Δϕm2​​.​
(15)
It is a global minimum within the chosen winding class: the integrand is strictly convex, and Jensen inequality bounds the functional below by (zB​−zA​)1+R2(Δϕm​/Δz)2​, with equality only for constant slope. Equivalently, unrolling the cylinder makes the minimizing path a straight segment.
The signed pitch of a helix, measured for an increase of 2π in angle, is
Pm​=Δϕm​2πΔz​.​
(16)
Its geometric magnitude is ∣Pm​∣. If only the physical endpoints are fixed, choose the integer m minimizing ∣Δϕm​∣; opposite points may give two equally short helices. If the lifted endpoint angles are prescribed, use that winding class. A zero angular increment gives a straight generator, the limiting infinite-pitch case.

The left boundary condition makes it ax on x<ξ, and the right Neumann boundary condition makes it constant b on x>ξ. Continuity gives b=aξ. Integrating the distributional equation through the Dirac delta function gives the jump Gx​(ξ+;ξ)−Gx​(ξ−;ξ)=1, so a=−1. Therefore
G(x;ξ)=−min(x,ξ)={−x,−ξ,​x≤ξ,x≥ξ.​​
(17)
Apply the Green function to the forcing:
y(x)=∫01​G(x;ξ)ξe−ξdξ=−∫0x​ξ2e−ξdξ−x∫x1​ξe−ξdξ.

Evaluation yields
y(x)=(x+2)e−x+e2x​−2.​

For a particle of mass m, the probability density and one-dimensional probability current are
ρ=ψ∗ψ,j=2miℏ​(ψ∗ψx​−ψψx∗​)=mℏ​Im(ψ∗ψx​).​
(20)
The Schrödinger equation and its complex conjugate, for real V, give
ρt​=ψt​ψ∗+ψψt∗​=2miℏ​(ψ∗ψxx​−ψψxx∗​)=−jx​.
(21)
The potential terms cancel precisely because V is real. Thus ρt​+jx​=0, the continuity equation for probability. Integrating over an interval says that its probability changes by the incoming current minus the outgoing current.

The global time-dependent phase cancels from the probability current. Put χ=eikx+Re−ikx. Direct multiplication gives
χ∗χx​=ik(1−∣R∣2)+ik(R∗e2ikx−Re−2ikx).
(22)
The second term is real, because the expression in parentheses is purely imaginary. Hence
j=mℏk​(1−∣R∣2).​
(23)
The first plane wave travels to the right with incident current ℏk/m; the second travels to the left with reflected current −(ℏk/m)∣R∣2. Their wave interference changes the probability density but cancels from the net current. The current vanishes for ∣R∣=1, is positive for ∣R∣<1, and is negative for ∣R∣>1. These plane waves are scattering states, not individually normalizable bound states.

Pi​(Tr​<∞)=qr.

n=0∑∞​Pi​(Xn​=i)=Pi​(Xn​=i for all n≥1)1​,​

They are self-adjoint operators, and α=α1​+iα2​. Conversely such a decomposition has α∗=α1​−iα2​. Expanding both products gives

ii

Words: 144 Articles: 1
10F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 144
ii OurBigBook.com
We prove the finite-dimensional spectral theorem for normal operators by induction on dimension. A complex linear operator has an eigenvector v with eigenvalue λ, by the fundamental theorem of algebra. For a normal operator T, the operator T−λI is also normal, and
∥(T−λI)w∥2=∥(T∗−λI)w∥2
(29)
for every w. Applying this to v shows T∗v=λv.
Normalize v. Its orthogonal complement W=v⊥ is invariant under both T and T∗: the adjoint operator identities pair Tw with v through T∗v, and T∗w with v through Tv. The restricted operator on W remains normal, and its adjoint is the restriction of T∗. Induction supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis of W, which together with v gives one for V.
Conversely, in an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, T is diagonal and T∗ is the diagonal matrix of the conjugate eigenvalues. The two diagonal operators commute. Thus normality is equivalent to an orthonormal eigenbasis. The zero-dimensional case is immediate.

Conversely let λ1​,…,λr​ be the distinct eigenvalues of a normal α. The orthonormal eigenbasis from part (ii) reduces the desired identity to g(λj​)=λj​. Lagrange interpolation polynomial provides the polynomial
g(z)=j=1∑r​λj​ℓ=j∏​λj​−λℓ​z−λℓ​​,α∗=g(α).​
(30)
Repeated eigenvalues cause no difficulty because interpolation uses only distinct values. If V={0}, use g=0. This proves both directions of the third equivalence.

An algebraic integer is a complex number satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. Let f∈Q[x] be the monic minimal polynomial of α. It is irreducible over Q. If H∈Z[x] is a monic polynomial vanishing at α, then f divides H over Q. Gauss lemma for polynomials implies that monic rational factors of a monic integer polynomial have integer coefficients. Thus f∈Z[x], and its irreducibility over Q implies irreducibility in Z[x].
For h∈Z[x] with h(α)=0, division by the monic f works in Z[x], giving h=qf+r with degr<degf. Since r(α)=0, minimality forces r=0. Conversely each multiple of f vanishes at α. Therefore
I=(f),Z[α]≅Z[x]/(f).​
(31)
Writing n=degf, division by f expresses every element uniquely as a0​+a1​α+⋯+an−1​αn−1 with integer coefficients. A relation among these powers would be a nonzero vanishing polynomial of degree less than n. Hence 1,α,…,αn−1 form a basis of the free module over Z Z[α].

Words: 173 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 173
b OurBigBook.com
The polynomial f(x)=x5+2x+2 satisfies the Eisenstein criterion at the prime two: every nonleading coefficient is divisible by two, and the constant coefficient is not divisible by four. Thus it is irreducible over Q and is the minimal polynomial of every one of its roots. Part (a) gives
Z[α]/(5)≅F5​[x]/(f​).
(32)
But
f(x)=(x−1)(x4+x3+x2+x+3)+5.
(33)
In the quotient, the two nonzero classes of x−1 and x4+x3+x2+x+3 multiply to zero. They are nonzero because their nonzero representative degrees are less than five. The quotient is not an integral domain, so (5) is not a prime ideal.
For ring homomorphisms preserving the identity, an image β of α in the Gaussian integers would satisfy f(β)=0. The minimal polynomial of β over Q would then be f, of degree five. This is impossible because β∈Q(i) has degree at most two. Thus there is no unital homomorphism Z[α]→Z[i]. If homomorphisms are instead allowed not to preserve the identity, the zero map exists; every nonzero homomorphism into this integral domain is unital, because the image of one is a nonzero idempotent and hence one.

The multiplicative field norm on this ring is
N(a+b−5​)=(a+b−5​)(a−b−5​)=a2+5b2.
(34)
If an element is a unit, its positive integer norm has a multiplicative inverse in the positive integers, hence is one. The only integer solutions of a2+5b2=1 are (a,b)=(1,0),(−1,0). Therefore the units are exactly 1 and −1.
The standard failure of unique factorization is
6=2⋅3=(1+−5​)(1−−5​).
(35)
There is no element of norm two or three: b=0 gives norm at least five, while b=0 gives a square. An alleged nontrivial factorization of 2 (norm four), 3 (norm nine), or 1±−5​ (norm six) would require a factor of norm two or three. Thus all four displayed factors are irreducible elements. No factor in the first factorization is associated to a factor in the second, since associates have the same norm and the norms are respectively four, nine and six. Hence Z[−5​] is not a unique factorization domain.

For a metric space (X,d), uniform continuity means
∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 ∀x,y∈X:d(x,y)<δ ⟹ ∣f(x)−f(y)∣<ε.
(36)
The choice of δ is independent of the points. A Lipschitz continuous function satisfies ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤Ld(x,y) for one finite constant L≥0. Choosing δ=ε/(L+1) proves Lipschitz continuity implies uniform continuity.
Let (xn​) be a Cauchy sequence. For a given ε>0, uniform continuity supplies δ>0, and the Cauchy property supplies N with d(xm​,xn​)<δ for m,n≥N. Then ∣f(xm​)−f(xn​)∣<ε, so (f(xn​)) is Cauchy in R. By completeness of the real numbers, (f(xn​)) converges, even if the original sequence has no limit in X.

Suppose the continuous f were not uniformly continuous. There would be an ε0​>0 and pairs xn​,yn​∈X with d(xn​,yn​)<1/n but ∣f(xn​)−f(yn​)∣≥ε0​. Sequential compactness gives a subsequence xnj​​→x∈X. The triangle inequality gives ynj​​→x as well. Continuity at x then gives f(xnj​​)−f(ynj​​)→0, a contradiction. Thus f is uniformly continuous.
It need not be Lipschitz continuous. On the sequentially compact interval [0,1], the continuous function f(x)=x​ has
∣x−0∣∣f(x)−f(0)∣​=x​1​→∞(x↓0).
(37)
No finite Lipschitz constant exists.

For each x∈X, density of Y allows a sequence yn​∈Y with d(yn​,x)<1/n. If f1​,f2​ are two continuous extensions, continuity gives
f1​(x)=limn​g(yn​)=f2​(x).
(38)
Thus a continuous extension is unique if it exists.
Now assume g is uniformly continuous. Each chosen yn​→x is a Cauchy sequence, so part (a), applied to Y, shows that g(yn​) converges in R. Define
f(x)=n→∞lim​g(yn​).​
(39)
This is independent of the choice: for another zn​→x in Y, d(yn​,zn​)→0, and uniform continuity gives g(yn​)−g(zn​)→0. At x∈Y, comparison with the constant sequence x proves f(x)=g(x).
To prove uniform continuity of the extension, choose δ>0 so that ∣g(y)−g(z)∣<ε/2 whenever y,z∈Y and d(y,z)<δ. If d(x,x′)<δ/3, choose sequences yn​→x and zn​→x′ in Y. For large n, both approximation distances are less than δ/3, so d(yn​,zn​)<δ. Passing to the limit gives ∣f(x)−f(x′)∣≤ε/2<ε. The same δ/3 works for all x,x′. Therefore the extension exists and is uniformly continuous. No completeness of X is needed; completeness of the target R is the relevant requirement.

Let T be a closed triangle contained, together with a neighbourhood, in the domain of a holomorphic function f. We prove Cauchy theorem for a triangle without assuming continuity of f′.
Join the edge midpoints to subdivide T into four triangles, each with half its diameter and perimeter. Their positively oriented contour integrals sum to the integral around T, because the internal edges cancel. At least one subtriangle has integral of modulus at least one quarter of the original. Repeat that choice to obtain nested closed triangles Tn​ satisfying
​∫∂T​f(z)dz​≤4n​∫∂Tn​​f(z)dz​,dn​=2−nd0​,Pn​=2−nP0​.
(40)
Their intersection is a single point z∗​, by compactness and shrinking diameter. complex differentiability at a point at z∗​ gives
f(z)=f(z∗​)+f′(z∗​)(z−z∗​)+(z−z∗​)r(z),r(z)→0.
(41)
The first two terms have polynomial primitives, hence integrate to zero around each triangle. For sufficiently large n, ∣r∣<ε on Tn​, so the complex line integral estimate gives
​∫∂Tn​​f(z)dz​≤εdn​Pn​.
(42)
Combining the bounds gives ∣∫∂T​f(z)dz∣≤εd0​P0​. Since ε is arbitrary,
∫∂T​f(z)dz=0.​
(43)
The orientation can be reversed with no change to the conclusion.

For every closed piecewise smooth curve γ in U, the winding number of f∘γ about zero is the integer
mγ​=2πi1​∫γ​f(z)f′(z)​dz.
(45)
If f=gkk​ for a holomorphic kth root, gk​ is nowhere zero, and
mγ​=k2πi1​∫γ​gk​gk′​​dz.
(46)
Thus mγ​ is divisible by every k for which a root exists. An infinite subset of the positive integers is unbounded, so a fixed integer divisible by all those k must be zero. Hence all periods of the holomorphic function f′/f vanish.
Fix z0​∈U. Since a domain is connected and open, its points can be joined by piecewise smooth paths. Vanishing periods make
H(z)=∫z0​z​f(w)f′(w)​dw
(47)
independent of path. It is a holomorphic primitive with H′=f′/f. Differentiating gives (fe−H)′=0, so fe−H=f(z0​). Choose a complex number c with ec=f(z0​). Then
F=H+c is holomorphic on U,f=eF.​
(48)
This constructs a global holomorphic logarithm without requiring U to be simply connected.

Cross-ratio conventions differ by permutations. Use the following ordering, which gives the signs requested in part (c):
r=[z1​,z2​,z3​,z4​]=(z1​−z2​)(z4​−z3​)(z1​−z4​)(z2​−z3​)​.​
(49)
Values involving infinity are defined by limits. This is the cross-ratio with second point mapped to zero: the Möbius transformation
T(z)=(z1​−z2​)(z−z4​)(z1​−z4​)(z−z2​)​
(50)
sends z1​,z2​,z4​ to 1,0,∞ and sends z3​ to r.
For M(z)=(az+b)/(cz+d), ad−bc=0, the identity
M(u)−M(v)=(cu+d)(cv+d)(ad−bc)(u−v)​
(51)
shows that all factors cancel in the cross-ratio. This proves Möbius invariance of the cross-ratio, with the cases involving infinity following by limits. Algebraic subtraction also gives
[z2​,z1​,z3​,z4​]=1−r=(z1​−z2​)(z3​−z4​)(z1​−z3​)(z2​−z4​)​.​
(52)
The latter expression is another common ordering for the cross-ratio; keeping the convention explicit prevents an incorrect reciprocal or sign.

Solution

Words: 109
b OurBigBook.com
With T from part (a), the first, second and fourth points map to 1,0,∞. The inverse image of the extended real line under a Möbius transformation is a generalized circle, meaning a circle or a line together with infinity. Thus, if r=T(z3​) is real, all four original points lie on that generalized circle.
Conversely, if the four points lie on one generalized circle, its image under T is another generalized circle containing 0,1,∞. A generalized circle containing infinity is a line, and the line through zero and one is the real line. Therefore T(z3​)=r is real. Hence the cross-ratio is real exactly when the four points are concyclic or collinear.

Kt​(x)=4πDt​1​e−x2/(4Dt).

Therefore θ(x,t)>0 for every real x and every t>0. Property P holds: diffusion has infinite propagation speed. The distant value can be extremely small, but is not zero. For the wave equation, introduce characteristic coordinates ξ=x−ct, η=x+ct when c=0. The equation becomes uξη​=0, so u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct). The initial conditions imply F+G=ϕ and −cF′+cG′=0. Constants can be absorbed into F,G, giving the D'Alembert formula

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Use the physical Coulomb bound state boundary condition: the spherically symmetric wavefunction is regular at the origin and square integrable with measure 4πr2dr. For E<0, set
K=ℏ−2mE​​>0.​
(61)
At large r, the decaying branch behaves exponentially as e−Kr. Substituting ψ=fe−Kr into the radial Schrödinger equation gives
rf′′+(2−2Kr)f′+2(λ−K)f=0.
(62)
The regular solution has a power series f(r)=∑j≥0​aj​rj, with recurrence
aj+1​=(j+1)(j+2)2[K(j+1)−λ]​aj​.​
(63)
A nonzero regular solution has a0​=0. If the series does not terminate, its coefficients eventually have one sign after choosing an overall real phase. For any fixed 0<δ<1/2 and sufficiently large j, the ratio of consecutive magnitudes is at least 2K(1−δ)/(j+2). The tail therefore grows at least as a positive constant times e2K(1−δ)r divided by a power of r; a finite polynomial of earlier terms cannot cancel it. Multiplication by e−Kr leaves exponential growth, contradicting normalizability.
Thus the series must terminate at degree N−1, where KN=λ and N is a positive integer. Conversely, termination gives a regular polynomial times e−λr/N, which is normalizable. Therefore
EN​=−2mN2ℏ2λ2​=−32π2ϵ02​ℏ2N2me4​,N=1,2,….​
(64)
These are the ℓ=0 members of the hydrogen spectrum. Regularity at the origin is essential: square integrability alone on the punctured radial interval would also admit a singular 1/r branch. Such a branch is not a physical eigenfunction of the ordinary three-dimensional Coulomb Hamiltonian; its singularity introduces an inadmissible point-source contribution. In the reduced radial variable u=rψ, the physical condition is u(0)=0.

b

Words: 78 Articles: 1
16B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 78
b OurBigBook.com
The agreement is in the energy levels, not in electron trajectories. The Bohr model assumes a particle on a circular orbit, with orbital angular momentum quantized as Nℏ. The Coulomb bound states here are spatially distributed wavefunctions with no definite classical orbit. Their probability density is spherically symmetric, and their orbital angular momentum is zero because ℓ=0. Their radial distributions also depend on N and can have nodes. A real radial wavefunction times a global stationary phase has zero probability current, unlike the circulating point charge in the Bohr picture.

For a moving closed circuit C(t) bounding an oriented surface S(t), Faraday's law is
Eem​(t)=∮C(t)​[E+v×B]⋅dl=−dtd​∫S(t)​B⋅ndS.​
(65)
Here E is the electric field, B the magnetic field, v the local velocity of a circuit element, and Eem​ the electromagnetic electromotive force per unit charge around the circuit. The line orientation and normal n obey the right-hand rule. The flux derivative is a total derivative and includes both changing field and changing surface. The term v×B is the motional electromotive force. A battery contributes an additional non-electromagnetic source electromotive force.

For E0​=0 and B0​=0, v=v0​e−t/τ and I=−(B0​L/R)v. The instantaneous Joule heating is
RI2=RB02​L2​v02​e−2t/τ=τmv02​​e−2t/τ.
(70)
Hence the energy dissipated up to time t and its infinite-time value are

(71)
The remaining kinetic energy is 21​mv02​e−2t/τ, so kinetic energy plus dissipated heat equals the initial kinetic energy at every time. The magnetic field redirects charge motion, and the circuit transfers mechanical energy to heat through the electric forces; there is no battery input in this case. If B0​=0, no current is induced, no energy is dissipated, and all the initial kinetic energy remains.

v

Words: 169 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 169
v OurBigBook.com
For motion to the right in B0​ez​, B0​>0, the induced current is clockwise. Its own magnetic field points into the page inside the circuit, opposing the increase in external flux, as required by Lenz's law. As that current changes, its changing flux also produces an electromotive force opposing the change in current: the circuit has inductance.
Consequently the algebraic current law used in parts (i)-(iv) must be replaced by a dynamical circuit equation that includes the derivative of the self-flux. The induced current cannot in general adjust instantaneously to the bar velocity. Energy is temporarily stored in the self-field and can later return to the motion or be dissipated; the simple exponential braking law can change. Self-field forces and changes of inductance with circuit geometry may also matter. The magnetic self-field changes the transient dynamics but does not create energy: mechanical energy, magnetic-field energy and Joule heat must be included in the conservation balance. A quantitative answer would require the circuit's inductance and its dependence on s.

ρ1​(φ1t​+21​∣∇φ1​∣2+gη)=ρ2​(φ2t​+21​∣∇φ2​∣2+gη).​

For a minimization problem over a domain D with inequality constraints gj​(x)≤0 and equality constraints hℓ​(x)=0, let
L(x,λ,μ)=f(x)+∑j​λj​gj​(x)+∑ℓ​μℓ​hℓ​(x).
(92)
The Lagrangian sufficiency theorem states: if x∗​ is feasible, λj​≥0, λj​gj​(x∗​)=0, and x∗​ globally minimizes L(⋅,λ,μ) on D, then x∗​ globally minimizes the constrained objective. Equality multipliers have no sign restriction.
For any feasible x, the sign of the inequality multipliers gives L(x,λ,μ)≤f(x). Feasibility and complementary slackness give L(x∗​,λ,μ)=f(x∗​). Therefore
f(x∗​)=L(x∗​,λ,μ)≤L(x,λ,μ)≤f(x).​
(93)
This proves the theorem. No convexity is necessary if the global minimization of the Lagrangian is already known. In a differentiable convex optimization problem with convex inequalities and affine equalities, a stationary point of this convex Lagrangian is automatically a global minimizer, which gives the familiar sufficiency of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions.

Its derivative at an interior index gives 5xi​−2xi−1​−2xi+1​=0, 1≤i<n. The terminal derivative gives 3xn​−2xn−1​=0. The characteristic equation 2r2−5r+2=0 has roots 2 and 1/2, so
xi​=a2i+b2−i,yi​=2a​2i−b2−i.

The conditions x0​=1 and 3xn​=2xn−1​ give a+b=1 and b=2⋅4na. Thus
a=1+2⋅4n1​,b=1+2⋅4n2⋅4n​,A=2(1+2⋅4n)1​,B=−1+2⋅4n2⋅4n​.​
(96)

For a direct application of Lagrangian sufficiency theorem, use equality constraints hi​=xi​−1−∑k=1i​yk​ and multipliers μi​=−2xi∗​. The Lagrangian derivatives in xi​ vanish. Its derivative in yj​ is 4yj∗​+2∑i=jn​xi∗​, which also vanishes: putting Sj​=2yj∗​+∑i=jn​xi∗​, the interior recurrence gives Sj​−Sj+1​=0, and the terminal condition gives Sn​=0. The Lagrangian has positive-definite quadratic part ∑i​(xi2​+2yi2​), so this stationary point is its unique global minimum. The candidate is feasible, and the theorem proves it is the unique constrained optimal solution. Equivalently, strict convexity of the eliminated objective proves the same global conclusion.
